course.title: Calculus I
course.description: A first course in single-variable calculus — from limits and continuity through derivatives, integrals, and the Fundamental Theorem that ties them together. Structure adapted from OpenStax Calculus Volume 1 (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: Evaluate lim(x->2) of (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2).
The derivative f'(x) is defined as…
questions.explanation: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient as h->0.

questions.prompt: Using the power rule, d/dx of x^3 is…
questions.explanation: d/dx x^n = n·x^(n-1), so d/dx x^3 = 3x^2.

questions.prompt: An antiderivative of x^2 is…
Evaluate integral from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links…
questions.explanation: It shows differentiation and integration are inverse processes.

questions.prompt: A function f is continuous at x = a when…
questions.explanation: Continuity requires the limit to exist and equal the function value at a.

questions.prompt: Compute d/dx of 5x.
questions.explanation: The derivative of a linear term c·x is the constant c, so d/dx(5x) = 5.

lessons.title: Limits and continuity
lessons.grammar_note: A limit describes where a function is heading, not necessarily where it lands.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Evaluate limits (including 0/0 forms by factoring) and test whether a function is continuous at a point. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, why can (x^2-4)/(x-2) have a limit at x=2 even though plugging in gives 0/0?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A limit answers: as x gets arbitrarily close to a, what value does f(x) approach? Substitution works when f is well-behaved, but a 0/0 form means algebra is hiding a removable factor. A function f is *continuous* at a when three things agree: f(a) is defined, lim(x->a) f(x) exists, and the two are equal. Worked example: lim(x->2) (x^2-4)/(x-2). Substituting gives 0/0, so factor the top: x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2). Cancel the (x-2): the expression equals x+2 for all x not equal to 2, and x+2 -> 4. So the limit is 4.

sections.heading: More worked examples
sections.text: Example A: lim(x->3) (x^2-9)/(x-3). Factor: (x-3)(x+3)/(x-3) = x+3 -> 3+3 = 6. Example B: lim(x->0) (x^2 + 3x)/x. Factor an x on top: x(x+3)/x = x+3 -> 0+3 = 3. Example C (continuity test): is f(x) = (x^2-1)/(x-1) continuous at x=1? The limit is (x-1)(x+1)/(x-1) = x+1 -> 2, but f(1) is 0/0, undefined. The limit exists yet f(1) does not, so f is *not* continuous at x=1 — this is a removable discontinuity, patched by defining f(1)=2.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: seeing 0/0 and declaring the limit undefined — 0/0 is a signal to factor, not a verdict. Mistake: assuming every function is continuous everywhere (removable and jump discontinuities exist). Exit: (a) What three conditions define continuity at a? (b) lim(x->2) (x^2-4)/(x-2) = ? Answers: f(a) defined, limit exists, and they are equal; 4.

lessons.title: The derivative: definition and rules
lessons.grammar_note: The derivative is a limit first and a rule second — the power rule is a shortcut the limit proves.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute a derivative from the limit definition and apply the power, constant-multiple, and sum rules. Warm-up: the derivative measures an instantaneous rate — what limit turns average rate into instantaneous rate?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The average rate of change of f over [x, x+h] is [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h. Shrinking h to zero gives the instantaneous rate — the *derivative*: f'(x) = lim(h->0) [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h. Worked example from the definition, f(x) = x^2: f(x+h) - f(x) = (x+h)^2 - x^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2 = 2xh + h^2. Divide by h: 2x + h. Let h -> 0: f'(x) = 2x. The general shortcut this proves is the *power rule*: d/dx x^n = n·x^(n-1).

sections.heading: More worked examples
sections.text: Example A (definition, f(x)=x^3): (x+h)^3 - x^3 = 3x^2·h + 3x·h^2 + h^3; divide by h to get 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2; as h->0 this is 3x^2, matching the power rule. Example B (sum and constant-multiple rules): d/dx (3x^2 + 5x) = 3·(2x) + 5·(1) = 6x + 5. Example C (fractional power): d/dx sqrt(x) = d/dx x^(1/2) = (1/2)·x^(-1/2) = 1/(2·sqrt(x)). Example D (evaluate a slope): for f(x)=x^2, f'(x)=2x, so the slope at x=3 is f'(3)=6.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing d/dx x^3 = 3x^3 — the exponent drops by one, giving 3x^2. Mistake: forgetting the constant term vanishes (d/dx of any constant is 0). Exit: (a) State the limit definition of f'(x). (b) d/dx (x^2 - 7x + 2) = ? Answers: lim(h->0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h; 2x - 7.

lessons.title: Applications of derivatives: rates and optimization
lessons.grammar_note: Set the derivative to zero to find candidates for maxima and minima — that is where the slope is flat.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use derivatives as rates of change and solve optimization problems by finding critical points. Warm-up: if position is s(t), what does s'(t) represent physically?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A derivative is a rate: if s(t) is position, velocity is s'(t). At a maximum or minimum of a smooth function, the tangent is horizontal, so f'(x) = 0; those x-values are *critical points*. Worked example (rate): s(t) = t^2 gives velocity v(t) = s'(t) = 2t, so at t = 3 the velocity is 6. Worked example (optimization): minimize f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3. Then f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0 gives x = 2, and f(2) = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1, the minimum value.

sections.heading: More worked examples
sections.text: Example A (classic fence problem): a farmer has 100 m of fencing for a rectangle; maximize area. With sides x and y, the perimeter is 2x + 2y = 100, so y = 50 - x. Area A(x) = x(50 - x) = 50x - x^2. Then A'(x) = 50 - 2x = 0 gives x = 25, y = 25, and maximum area A = 25·25 = 625 m^2 (a square). Example B (critical points): f(x) = x^3 - 3x has f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0, so x^2 = 1 and x = 1 or x = -1. Example C (second derivative sign): for f(x)=x^2-4x+3, f''(x)=2 > 0, confirming x=2 is a minimum.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Solve: (1) if s(t)=t^3, find velocity at t=2; (2) find the critical point of f(x)=x^2 - 6x + 5; (3) maximize A(x)=x(20 - x); (4) find all critical points of f(x)=x^3 - 12x. Answers: (1) v(t)=3t^2, so v(2)=12; (2) f'(x)=2x-6=0 gives x=3; (3) A'(x)=20-2x=0 gives x=10 and A=10·10=100; (4) f'(x)=3x^2-12=0 gives x^2=4, so x=2 or x=-2.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting the critical x-value as the answer to an optimization problem when the question asks for the maximum value — plug x back in. Mistake: forgetting a rectangle's perimeter has two of each side (2x + 2y). Exit: (a) What equation locates critical points? (b) For A(x)=x(50-x), which x gives the max? Answers: f'(x)=0; x=25.

questions.prompt: Evaluate lim(x->3) of (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3).
Differentiate x^4.
questions.explanation: Power rule: d/dx x^4 = 4x^3.

questions.prompt: The critical point of f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 is at x =…
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0 gives x = 2.

questions.prompt: Compute d/dx of (x^2 - 7x).
questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term: 2x - 7.

questions.prompt: A rectangle with perimeter 20 has sides x and 10 - x. Which x maximizes the area x(10 - x)?
questions.explanation: A'(x) = 10 - 2x = 0 gives x = 5, so a 5-by-5 square.

questions.prompt: f is continuous at x = a only if…
questions.explanation: The limit must exist and equal the value f(a).

lessons.title: Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
lessons.grammar_note: Integration undoes differentiation — the definite integral evaluates an antiderivative at the endpoints.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Find antiderivatives, evaluate definite integrals with the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC), and differentiate an integral. Warm-up: if d/dx of x^3 is 3x^2, what function has derivative x^2?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An *antiderivative* F satisfies F'(x) = f(x); the reverse power rule is integral(x^n) dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not equal to -1. The FTC (Part 2) turns antiderivatives into exact areas: integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). The FTC (Part 1) says differentiating an integral gives the integrand back: d/dx integral from a to x of f(t) dt = f(x). Worked example: integral from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx. An antiderivative is F(x) = x^3/3, so the value is F(2) - F(0) = 8/3 - 0 = 8/3.

sections.heading: More worked examples
sections.text: Example A: integral from 1 to 3 of 2x dx. Antiderivative F(x) = x^2, so F(3) - F(1) = 9 - 1 = 8. Example B: integral from 0 to 1 of 3x^2 dx. Antiderivative F(x) = x^3, so F(1) - F(0) = 1 - 0 = 1. Example C (trig): integral from 0 to pi of sin(x) dx. Antiderivative F(x) = -cos(x), so F(pi) - F(0) = -cos(pi) - (-cos(0)) = -(-1) - (-1) = 1 + 1 = 2. Example D (FTC Part 1): d/dx integral from 2 to x of sqrt(t) dt = sqrt(x) — differentiating the integral simply returns the integrand.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Evaluate: (1) integral(x^3) dx; (2) integral from 0 to 3 of x^2 dx; (3) integral from 1 to 2 of 4x dx; (4) integral from 0 to pi of sin(x) dx; (5) d/dx integral from 0 to x of t^2 dt. Answers: (1) x^4/4 + C; (2) [x^3/3] = 27/3 - 0 = 9; (3) [2x^2] = 2·4 - 2·1 = 8 - 2 = 6; (4) [-cos(x)] = -cos(pi) + cos(0) = 1 + 1 = 2; (5) x^2 by FTC Part 1.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dropping the + C on an indefinite integral (the antiderivative is a whole family). Mistake: sign slips with -cos(x) — remember integral(sin x) dx = -cos(x) + C. Exit: (a) State FTC Part 2. (b) integral from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx = ? Answers: integral from a to b of f = F(b) - F(a) where F' = f; 8/3.

lessons.title: Applications of integration: area
lessons.grammar_note: Area under a curve is a definite integral; area between two curves subtracts the lower from the upper.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute the area under a curve and the area between two curves using definite integrals. Warm-up: which integral gives the area under f(x) on [a, b]?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For f(x) >= 0 on [a, b], the area under the curve is integral from a to b of f(x) dx. For two curves with f(x) >= g(x) on [a, b], the area between them is integral from a to b of [f(x) - g(x)] dx — top minus bottom. Worked example: area under f(x) = x^2 on [0, 3]. That is integral from 0 to 3 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] from 0 to 3 = 27/3 - 0 = 9.

sections.heading: More worked examples
sections.text: Example A (check against geometry): area under f(x) = x on [0, 4] is integral from 0 to 4 of x dx = [x^2/2] = 16/2 - 0 = 8 — which matches the triangle area (1/2)·4·4 = 8. Example B (area between curves): between y = x (upper) and y = x^2 (lower) on [0, 1], since x >= x^2 there, the area is integral from 0 to 1 of (x - x^2) dx = [x^2/2 - x^3/3] from 0 to 1 = (1/2 - 1/3) - 0 = 1/6. Example C: area under f(x) = 2x on [1, 3] is integral from 1 to 3 of 2x dx = [x^2] = 9 - 1 = 8.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Compute: (1) area under y = x^2 on [0, 2]; (2) area under y = 2x on [0, 3]; (3) area under y = 3x^2 on [0, 2]; (4) area between y = x and y = x^2 on [0, 1]. Answers: (1) [x^3/3] = 8/3; (2) [x^2] = 9 - 0 = 9; (3) [x^3] = 8 - 0 = 8; (4) integral(x - x^2) = [x^2/2 - x^3/3] = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: subtracting in the wrong order for area between curves (always top minus bottom, or you get a negative area). Mistake: forgetting to evaluate at both limits — an area needs F(b) - F(a), not just F(b). Exit: (a) What integral gives the area between f (upper) and g (lower)? (b) Area under y=x^2 on [0,3] = ? Answers: integral from a to b of [f(x) - g(x)] dx; 9.

items.example: lim(x->2) (x^2-4)/(x-2) = 4, even though direct substitution gives 0/0.

items.translation: the property that a function has no breaks: lim(x->a) f(x) equals f(a)
items.example: A polynomial is continuous at every point.

items.translation: the instantaneous rate of change, defined as lim(h->0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h
a function F whose derivative is f, written integral(f) dx = F + C
items.example: An antiderivative of x^2 is x^3/3 + C.

items.translation: the signed area under f from a to b, equal to F(b) - F(a)
items.example: integral from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx = 8/3.

items.translation: the result that differentiation and integration are inverse operations
items.example: It lets us evaluate integral from a to b of f as F(b) - F(a).

questions.explanation: Reverse power rule: x^(3+1)/(3+1) + C = x^4/4 + C.

questions.prompt: Evaluate integral from 1 to 3 of 2x dx.
questions.explanation: Antiderivative x^2, so 3^2 - 1^2 = 9 - 1 = 8.

questions.prompt: By the FTC, d/dx integral from 0 to x of t^2 dt equals…
questions.explanation: FTC Part 1 returns the integrand evaluated at x: x^2.

questions.prompt: The area under y = x^2 on [0, 3] is…
questions.explanation: integral from 0 to 3 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] = 27/3 = 9.

questions.prompt: Evaluate integral from 0 to pi of sin(x) dx.
The area between y = x and y = x^2 on [0, 1] is…
questions.explanation: integral from 0 to 1 of (x - x^2) dx = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.

lessons.title: Applied project: model a real rate of change

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a real quantity that changes over time — a car's distance, a savings balance, water filling a tank — and model it with a simple function. You will connect its derivative (a rate) and its integral (an accumulated total), then interpret both in plain words.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Write a function, e.g. distance s(t) = t^2 (in meters, t in seconds). 2) Differentiate to get the rate s'(t) and state its units (here velocity 2t, in m/s). 3) Pick an interval [a, b] and compute a definite integral that accumulates something meaningful (e.g. integral from 0 to 3 of the velocity 2t dt = [t^2] = 9 meters travelled). 4) Write one sentence explaining what the derivative and the integral each tell you about your quantity.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check your work with these: your function is stated with units; the derivative is computed correctly with the power rule; the definite integral is evaluated as F(b) - F(a), not left as an antiderivative; and your final sentence correctly names the derivative as a rate and the integral as an accumulated total. If all four hold, you have shown how the two halves of calculus describe the same changing quantity.
